summary.title: Dimeric cyclobutane formation under continuous flow conditions using organophotoredox catalysed [2+2]-cycloaddition
summary.authors: Helena F Grantham; Marc C Kimber; M F C Grantham; Kimber
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalyzed dimerization of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinylcarbazoles and styrenes, to synthesize valuable cyclobutane dimers. By merging homogenous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology, the authors address limitations inherent in traditional batch methods, such as excessive reaction times, high catalyst loadings, and the need for cryogenic conditions. The optimized flow conditions utilize a commercial platform with a catalyst loading as low as 0.1 mol% and irradiation at 450 nm. The methodology was successfully applied to synthesize 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) and a series of functionalized analogues, achieving higher isolated yields and significantly shorter reaction times compared to batch protocols. Furthermore, the approach was extended to the synthesis of lignan natural products like magnosalin without the requirement for cryogenic temperatures. The work demonstrates that continuous flow technology enhances the efficiency, scalability, and substrate scope of radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloadditions, offering a robust route to functional materials and natural products.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a continuous flow protocol for the organophotoredox-catalyzed dimerization of electron-rich alkenes, specifically vinylcarbazoles and styrenes, to synthesize valuable cyclobutane dimers. By merging homogenous small-molecule organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow technology, the authors address limitations inherent in traditional batch methods, such as excessive reaction times, high catalyst loadings, and the need for cryogenic conditions. The optimized flow conditions utilize a commercial platform with a catalyst loading as low as 0.1 mol% and irradiation at 450 nm. The methodology was successfully applied to synthesize 1,2-transdicarbazylcyclobutane (t-DCzCB) and a series of functionalized analogues, achieving higher isolated yields and significantly shorter reaction times compared to batch protocols. Furthermore, the approach was extended to the synthesis of lignan natural products like magnosalin without the requirement for cryogenic temperatures. The work demonstrates that continuous flow technology enhances the efficiency, scalability, and substrate scope of radical cation-initiated [2+2]-cycloadditions, offering a robust route to functional materials and natural products.

Research Context
Cyclobutane dimers are valuable for functional materials and natural products. Radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition is the key mechanism. Organophotoredox catalysis offers sustainability advantages over metal catalysts. Traditional batch organophotoredox dimerizations suffer from excessive reaction times. Batch methods often require cryogenic conditions and high catalyst loadings. Continuous flow technology improves irradiation efficiency in photochemical reactions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can continuous flow improve the efficiency of organophotoredox dimerization? Will flow conditions reduce catalyst loading and reaction time compared to batch? Can this method synthesize functionalized cyclobutanes and natural products? Is the continuous flow protocol scalable to multi-millimole scales? Will flow conditions eliminate the need for cryogenic temperatures?

Methodological Details
The study compared continuous flow versus batch reaction conditions. A commercial, off-the-shelf, continuous flow platform was used. Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB used 3 mol% catalyst and deoxygenated acetone. Batch synthesis required cryogenic temperatures and extended reaction times. Optimal continuous flow synthesis used 0.5 mL.min-1 flow rate. The residence time for optimal conditions was 20 minutes. Irradiation was performed at 450 nm wavelength. Catalyst loading was optimized at 2 mol% for the initial study. HPLC-analysis with p-terphenyl as internal standard was used for optimization. Substrates were dissolved in acetone at 0.4 M concentration for optimization. For substituted substrates, concentration was reduced to 0.2 M. Flow rates were adjusted to 0.2 mL.min-1 for substituted substrates. The study examined brominated, chloro, methoxy, and hydroxy substituted vinylcarbazoles. Electron relays like anthracene were used for styrene dimerization. Magnosalin synthesis was performed on a 10 mmol scale.

Procedures And Architectures
The mechanism involves generation of an alkene radical cation intermediate. The radical cation undergoes [2+2]-cycloaddition to form a cyclobutyl radical cation. The cyclobutyl radical cation is subsequently reduced to the dimeric cyclobutane. The organophotoredox catalyst (10) initiates the radical cation formation. The flow system utilized a commercial platform with specific flow rates. Irradiation sources were tested at 405 nm, 420 nm, and 450 nm. Control experiments confirmed the necessity of catalyst and irradiation. Background oxidation by adventitious oxygen was identified as a side reaction. Vinyl carbazoles were synthesized via the method of Obora and coworkers. Brominated products were used for Suzuki crosscoupling and borylation. Styrene dimerization required an electron relay to suppress polymerization. Anthracene was added to the starting solution before introduction into the apparatus.

Key Results
Batch synthesis of t-DCzCB achieved 82% isolated yield. Optimal flow conditions achieved 93% yield with 2 mol% catalyst. Increasing catalyst to 4.5 mol% resulted in 90% yield. Reducing flow rate to 2 mL.min-1 decreased yield to 79%. Reducing flow rate to 0.1 mL.min-1 dropped yield to 53%. Carbazole formation was observed at low flow rates due to oxygen. 10 mmol scale synthesis achieved 79% yield with 0.1 mol% catalyst. Flow dimerization of 3-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave 64% yield vs 48% batch. Flow dimerization of 4-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave 71% yield vs 31% batch. Flow dimerization of 3,6-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole gave 65% yield. Flow dimerization of 2-chloro-9-vinylcarbazole gave 61% yield. Flow dimerization of 2-methoxy-9-vinylcarbazole gave 45% yield. Flow dimerization of 3,6-di-tert-butyl-9-vinylcarbazole gave 57% yield. Flow dimerization of 3,6-bisarylated 9-vinyl carbazole gave 50% yield. Flow dimerization of 4-methoxy styrene gave 44% yield. Flow dimerization of styrene 29 with diethylaniline gave 22% yield. Flow dimerization of E-aserone gave 40% yield of magnosalin. Suzuki coupling of 13b gave 75% yield. Borylation of 13b gave 36% yield.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Continuous flow enhances irradiation efficiency leading to higher conversions. Flow conditions allow for significantly reduced reaction times. Low catalyst loadings approach the efficiency of Ru-based systems. The method enables synthesis of functionalized cyclobutanes previously difficult to access. Flow conditions facilitate the synthesis of natural products without cryogenics. The protocol demonstrates scalability for industrial application.

Contradictions And Limitations
Solubility of substrates in acetone proved challenging at 0.4 M. Concentration had to be reduced to 0.2 M for substituted substrates. 1-bromo-9-vinylcarbazole proved very challenging with no product detected. 2,7-dibromo-9-vinylcarbazole showed batch slightly outperforming flow. 2-arylated vinylcarbazoles showed poor solubility affecting yield. Background oxidation by oxygen reduced yields at low flow rates. Yields for some styrene derivatives were modest compared to carbazoles.

Claims
Continuous flow organophotoredox catalysis provides a superior route to cyclobutane dimers compared to batch methods. Flow conditions provided improved isolated yields. Reaction times were considerably shorter in flow. Catalyst loading was greatly reduced. Some substrates performed better in batch. Solubility issues limited flow performance for some substrates. The method enables scalable synthesis of functional materials.
The methodology is applicable to the synthesis of lignan natural products. Magnosalin was synthesized on a 10 mmol scale. No cryogenic temperatures were required. Yields for natural products were modest compared to carbazoles. The protocol expands the utility of organophotoredox catalysis.

Data And Code Availability
Full details of HPLC calibration can be found in the supporting information.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments confirmed the necessity of catalyst and irradiation. Lowering flow rate exacerbated yield reduction. Background oxidation was identified as a cause for yield loss at low flow.

Ethical Considerations
The study utilized organophotoredox catalysis for sustainability.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 details the optimization study of flow rate, catalyst loading, and wavelength. Scheme 1 illustrates cyclobutane dimers as functional materials and natural products. Scheme 2 depicts the radical cation-induced [2+2]-cycloaddition mechanism. Scheme 3 shows the merging of organophotoredox catalysis with continuous flow.

Three Takeaways
Continuous flow enables low catalyst loading and high yields. The method provides a scalable route to natural products. Flow conditions eliminate the need for cryogenic temperatures.
